title: Could inverter restrictions slow solar and energy storage development in the EU?
gist: New European Commission restrictions on inverters from 'high-risk' countries including China threaten EU solar PV and energy storage deployment, since Chinese suppliers held more than 80% of European inverter shipments in 2025. Wood Mackenzie (in a SolarPower Europe-commissioned report, promoted in this short teaser) flags Central and Eastern Europe and utility-scale solar and storage as most exposed to higher costs, procurement problems, delays and cancellations through 2030.

insights.claim: Chinese suppliers accounted for more than 80% of European inverter shipments in 2025, so European Commission restrictions on inverters from high-risk countries including China hit the dominant source of supply for EU solar and storage.
insights.speaker: Anna  Darmani
insights.so_what: Concentration above 80% means any binding EU restriction forces large-scale supplier switching; watch the final scope and timing of the Commission's high-risk vendor rules.
insights.quote: Chinese suppliers accounted for more than 80% of European inverter shipments in 2025.
insights.locator: Chinese suppliers accounted for more than 80%

insights.claim: Restrictions on Chinese and other high-risk-country inverters raise questions beyond equipment availability, including the loss of established sales and aftersales infrastructure, higher project costs and longer development timelines for European solar PV and storage projects.
insights.speaker: Anna  Darmani
insights.so_what: Aftersales and service networks are a hidden switching cost; installed-base service exposure matters as much as new procurement for asset owners.
insights.locator: New restrictions on inverters from countries considered as high-risk

themes.theme: Cost and supply squeeze on developers

insights.claim: European utilities and developers switching to alternative non-Chinese inverter suppliers face higher costs and limited availability that could further pressure already-tight solar and storage project economics, even as supply from Western manufacturers grows.
insights.speaker: Anna  Darmani
insights.so_what: Western inverter makers gain pricing power in Europe while developer margins compress; the open question the report poses is whether non-Chinese manufacturing capacity can meet the demand shift.
insights.quote: higher costs and limited availability could put further pressure on already-tight project economics, despite growing available supply from Western manufacturers
insights.locator: For utilities and developers looking to alternative suppliers

insights.claim: Rising inverter costs and supply constraints in the EU could affect commissioning timelines and the viability of planned solar and storage capacity, raising the risk of project delays or cancellations and lowering deployment forecasts through 2030 depending on the policy scenario.
insights.speaker: Anna  Darmani
insights.so_what: EU solar and storage pipeline forecasts carry policy-driven downside; track project cancellations and delay rates as inverter rules firm up.
insights.locator: Rising equipment costs and supply constraints

themes.theme: Uneven exposure by region and segment

insights.claim: The impact of EU inverter restrictions varies significantly by market and project type: Central and Eastern Europe is particularly exposed, and utility-scale solar and energy storage projects could face procurement challenges as developers look beyond established Chinese suppliers.
insights.speaker: Anna  Darmani
insights.so_what: Central and Eastern European solar and storage pipelines, and utility-scale developers, carry the most concentrated risk from inverter supplier restrictions.
insights.quote: Central and Eastern Europe is particularly exposed
insights.locator: How could inverter restrictions affect solar and storage projects?
